utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start, I used the word "almost insurmountable" last week. If one doesn't move to the mountain, sometimes the mountains move toward us. There is a fair chance but it will be confirmed either today or tomorrow that we might be not sitting in the week preferred by both parties, and that would be the week of the 11th of October. I would say there is a 90 per cent chance that we'll manage to achieve that. Mr. Harmon, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are. Our next witness is Mr. Stjepan Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Kljuic comes into court, I wonder if I could just say something and be clear about the way in which we are proceeding -- well, with specifically this witness but it may be a point of more general application. A draft or an 89(F) statement has been prepared in relation to Mr. Kljuic, but the Defence expresses its concern that the original purpose of the -- if you like the special 89(F) procedure which was thrashed out for the purposes of this case is in danger of being misused. The starting point for that was that in relation to any witness where there was a longish statement, there would inevitably be parts of the statement which were not likely seriously to be in contention, not likely to be seriously capable of challenge by the Defence and really rather pointless and time-consuming to draw out with elaborate oral examination-in-chief. It followed from that, though, that because there might be fairly substantial passages which were dealt with then by, really, reference to a statement, that those outside the Court would have no idea what was going on in relation to those passages. So the remedy was to produce a piece of concise information for the general public to enable them to see what had happened, and that was the purpose. We seem to be creeping and more than creeping, we seem to be moving quite fast to the procedure being used for a quite different purpose, which is, of course, to save time but to save time in a way which is driving everything then too far, because the idea was not that we should go beyond and trespass beyond those relatively non-contentious areas and start using the 89(F) procedure as some equivalent, and this was mentioned in relation last week I think to a different witness as some equivalent to 92 bis and some way of going into and presenting more contentious and -- I say more significant; all the evidence we hope is significant -- but more contentious evidence going into the more significant areas without exploring them pouring in examination-in-chief. And we do submit, Your Honour, that over the last few weeks alone, it's been consistently demonstrated that there is potentially an enormous gap between what a witness says and signs up to in a written statement and what the witness actually says if that matter is explored in direct examination in chief. Of course some of our cross-examination has been directed to that. But we believe, Your Honour, that that has been, and we submit that that has been consistently and clearly showed. In other words, that we have demonstrated the severe dangers of assuming that what a witness says in a written statement in relation to important matters is in fact and would in fact represent the evidence that he would give. So with that general comment, but specifically in relation to this witness, we do particularly invite the Tribunal to ensure, please, that this 89(F) procedure which we have worked out is only used for its original purpose and that great care is taken that it does not creep into that other area altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Let one thing be clear, that you perfectly set out what the purpose of the whole 89(F) summaries is. The summaries are not in evidence. It's just to inform the public. And therefore, if there is any contentious issue, or at least if there is any issue on which the witness would testify different from what his written statement says, then the Prosecution could either choose to leave out certain parts, especially contentious issues, from the 89(F) statements. It could indicate that, for example, that the witness gave his statement and will testify and then just mention the subject rather than to what exactly the contest is so that the public is able to follow. And this brings me to another observation, and that is that in the view of the Chamber and, I think, having seen some of the 89(F) summaries, the Chamber has indicated that it thinks that the summary for the public could be far shorter and less in detail. Let's leave the details to the examination-in-chief where it needs further attention. If the 89(F) statement as such is not contentious, then of course it's the statement which is then in evidence or any relevant parts in evidence. So I think we still have to -- we have to be very precise to that extent. The Chamber agrees with you. We have to be -- we have to keep clearly in mind what the summary is -- what the statement is. If the statement differs from what the Prosecution expects, that would be the testimony that should then not be confused in one way or the other, and finally that the summary serves this specific purpose of enabling the public not to lose track of what happens in this courtroom. Mr. Harmon, I don't know whether you'd like to add anything to that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'd like to proceed with the witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But on the other hand, it is a concern which is expressed and which needs proper attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just very briefly clarify what is the distinction from the Defence point of view. We endorse, with respect, everything that Your Honour has just said. So far as the 89(F) summary is concerned, in a sense the Defence's concerns are no greater or no less than anybody else's in court. That's simply to keep the public informed. So it's not really -- it's not an issue between the Prosecution and the Defence. What's more important from the Defence's point of view is that it is clear to us which bits of the statements the Prosecution are intending not to explore in oral examination-in-chief and which they are intending to explore. And the 89(F) summary -- the shorter it is the more this is true -- only in the barest terms gives us that indication. So the 89(F) summary is almost irrelevant from the Defence's actual working purposes. The important thing is that this clear distinction is drawn and we have some firm indication as to which areas of the statement the Prosecution is not proposing to explore in examination-in-chief so that we have the chance to make submissions in relation to that at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see what is the case in relation to this witness. You've specifically drawn our attention to that. We will pay that attention to the issue. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By your answer, I do establish that you hear me in a language you understand. Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher now hands out text of this declaration. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Kljuic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be provided with a copy of Prosecution Exhibits 291 and 292, a copy of his statement and a binder with intercepts and his comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, while these documents are being distributed, let me begin by asking you about your background in part. Once these documents have been distributed I will interrupt and then I will continue with a further description of your background. Mr. Kljuic, you were born in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1939. What I'm going to do is ask you to affirm what I say at the appropriate moment. You were born in Sarajevo on the 19th of December, 1939. You are a Bosnian Croat. You studied literature at the University of Sarajevo. By profession, you were a journalist from 1964 until 1971. You were a journalist for the newspaper Oslobodjenje in Sarajevo, and from 1971 until 1990, you were a correspondent for the Croatian newspaper Vjesnik, but you were reporting from Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, I'm going to come back to further details about your background and your political career in particular, but you have before you a Prosecution Exhibit which is a statement that was given by you on the 18th of April, 2001; the 23rd of May, 2001; and the 5th of December, 2002. You have had a chance to review this statement, have you not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, other than one correction which you pointed out to me which is found in paragraph 53, which is the last line in 53, in the English translation of that statement the last word should not be the word "state," it should be the word "town." So the sentence should read, "He had one foot in the country and one foot in the town." Is that the correction that you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So do you, therefore, affirm your statement before this Court?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of Prosecution Exhibit 292, which is a binder with intercepts, let me review that with you briefly. Mr. Kljuic, while you were here in The Hague before testifying, did you have an opportunity to listen to a number of intercepts, and were you asked to either make comments on them as well as identify the voices of the speakers to the extent that you were able to do so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I listened to the intercepts. I identified the people I was able to. I identified, and I also made several comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if you turn to the binder which is Prosecution Exhibit 292, if you open it up you will see first there is a declaration signed by you. If you turn to the next page, you will see a spreadsheet that has --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [In English] Stop, please. I have French language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now in the Bosnian language, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now this -- I'd like to take you through this Prosecution Exhibit 292. There has been prepared a spreadsheet on which it identifies the specific intercept by number. On the left-hand side there is a KID ID, and you will see that each of the intercepts thereafter has a tab associated with a particular intercept. The speaker that you were able to identify is identified in a column. Then that is text that contains your comments. And your signature appears on the first page of this spreadsheet, 17 pages long, and your initials appear thereafter on each of the pages. Do you adopt, then, the comments that are contained in this particular spreadsheet? And there are two other similar spreadsheets that were prepared. Do you adopt your comments contained in those particular spreadsheets?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the comments that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a very thinly disguised way of giving a very large body of evidence by written statement without going through the proper procedures. A considerable proportion of this witness's evidence, apparently, relates to these intercepts. We were supplied with a very large -- or a list of a very large number of intercepts, as it happens, for the witness. We raise the other question which is why on earth we've been supplied with this list so recently. These comments, I believe I'm right, that we even had them over the weekend, this particular schedule, which makes it completely impossible to get it to Mr. Krajisnik anyway. So we turn up on the first morning of court with this witness's detailed comments on a large number of intercepts not having -- it's helpfully -- there is a column in B/C/S, but without our client having had a chance to look. So we do raise the question why on earth couldn't have been done while Mr. Kljuic was back in his own country. I presume he didn't require a last-minute input here. But it is, to go back to the essential point, this is effectively, in this area, the witness preparing or somebody preparing a substantial and detailed written statement and just getting into the witness box and saying, "Yes, I confirm my statement." So it's equivalent to 92 bis or it's equivalent to 89(F) and it's simply not the way these matters should be dealt with, leaving aside the practical difficulty that I have indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have identified for the Defence a potential list of intercepts about two and a half weeks ago, if I'm not mistaken. I provided that list to the Defence. Mr. Stewart had ample opportunity to review those potential intercepts as well -- I'm sorry. And then subsequently I provided to the witness, after Mr. Kljuic arrived, the comments that Mr. Kljuic made on those intercepts. Once Mr. Kljuic had narrowed down from the potential list of intercepts that I had selected, I provided to the Defence -- I wish I had brought my notes as to when I provided these. I provided before the weekend, the 17-page list of intercepts and comments to the Defence. I informed the Defence that there were additional intercepts that I needed to have Mr. Kljuic review, which he did. Then there needed to be translations of those comments so the Defence could have them in a language, and yesterday afternoon, I believe, I provided the next and final list which was ten intercepts to the Defence. I provide that had to them sometime around noon yesterday. The situation is this, Your Honour: The witness is here for a limited period of time. The intercepts can be played one at a time. His testimony can be protracted. That's not the most efficient way to proceed, in our view. Our position is that Mr. Kljuic has had an opportunity to listen to these intercepts. He has made his comments. These intercepts have been provided to the Defence weeks ago. There was ample opportunity for the Defence to consult with their client about the intercepts, and we believe that this is an efficient and fair way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've got two issues as far as I see. The first one is time; the second one is whether this is the way to proceed with 89(F) statements. Mr. Harmon, I don't think I'm mistaking when I say that the requirement under Rule 92 bis, as far as the act and the conduct of the accused is concerned, also applies in respect of 89(F). And I noted that it seems that the intercepts deal to a large extent with -- well, what one could say is act and conduct of the accused. That's what he did at that time. So to that extent, I think it would be fair to stick to the case law of this Tribunal, that is, not to introduce just by his and other comments especially not if they are related to the words spoken at that time, at least as it appears from the transcript by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's my intention to introduce a number of these intercepts, to play them in Court, to have Mr. Krajisnik hear them, to have Mr. Stewart hear them and have Mr. Kljuic comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my first comment -- I don't want to have an unseemly squabble about it. Mr. Harmon wishes he brought his notes with him, et cetera. We wish he brought his notes with him because a little more care needs to be take been the timetable. Mr. Harmon says weeks ago. The 10th of September, which was sixteen days ago, was the first notification that we were given that this witness was going to be giving evidence during this phase of the trial at all. On the 17th of September, we were given a list of 137 or 138 intercepts. The detailed summary which we're talking about now and which we're looking at with this witness's comments were supplied on Saturday. Mr. Harmon asked me -- he very kindly telephoned me. We had a couple of short telephone calls. He courteously telephoned me he asked if I had any objection about that being passed on I think in accordance with the Court's requests to the Court. I indicated to him that I didn't have any objection but that I hadn't read them. I just take the view that if of course for any reason the material should be withdrawn from the Trial Chamber a professional Bench doesn't have a problem with that. So I didn't want to slow things down by saying oh, no, give me time to read it before you even pass on the material to the Trial Chamber, but I made it clear I hadn't. This timetable is really quite different from -- well, from Mr. Harmon's apparent recollection of it. The weekend when we're coming up with this witness is not the ideal time, and it does not give Mr. Krajisnik the opportunity. We don't wish, Your Honour, as far as it can possibly be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm just pausing because I can see Your Honour is conferring with his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We say we don't wish to have unnecessary playing of tapes or disks of the actual telephone conversation. It will be necessary from time to time, but we don't want that to be done just for the sake of doing it. But there is an intermediate stage. After all, we have transcripts as well, so some combination -- but, Your Honour, we've made our point as to how we submit this matter should be dealt with but we don't want to say that the actual timetable is a little different, if it ever became necessary to explore that in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add one suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that is this. I'll make one observation first. Mr. Kljuic, if possible, needs to conclude his testimony and be in Sarajevo on Thursday. This is a discussion that we should have and perhaps we could have after Court and after his testimony in any particular day. My suggestion is this, Your Honour: If there is a particular intercept that the Defence identifies that goes to the acts and conduct of the accused that it specifically wants to have Mr. Kljuic comment on or have it played in front of him, I'm more than happy to have any intercept that they find objectionable on that basis played before this Court while Mr. Kljuic is here. He can provide his comments viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- may I say, Your Honour, that isn't quite the point. We assume out of those 138 intercepts the Prosecution have made a selection. I'm not sure exactly what the total is, but it's more like -- I don't know whether it's 17. Maybe that's just one list but it's in the nature of 20 or 30 or something like that. I may stand to be corrected on the detail but, you know, it's of that order. We rather assume that the Prosecution have selected those intercepts because they regard those as more significant to their case. All the intercepts are within the category of acts and conduct of the accused because these are conversations to which the accused was a party, whatever the precise topic of the conversation. So when we have intercepts which the Prosecution have identified as sufficiently significant to make that selection, in principle, in relation to each of those intercepts the evidence should be given what we would call in summary properly. That doesn't necessarily require them to be played at length, because we do have transcripts. So a witness's explanation of what he understands and legitimate comments that he can make can in many cases be made by reference to the transcript but that is -- the transcript of the conversation, but that is a wholly different exercise from simply preparing a batch of comments and saying, "Yes, those are my comments," and handing them over on what we have already made our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I already gave some guidance to Mr. Harmon in that respect. The Chamber, of course, is concerned about this way of preparation, not primarily blaming the Prosecution because the Chamber, is aware that as the Defence, the Prosecution has also its time restraints. We'll now proceed, and on the basis of what we hear, we'll then decide whether additional time or facilities should be given or whether a recall would be appropriate at a later stage. But let's first see with the guidance the Chamber just gave to Mr. Harmon where we -- in what direction we go and whether there's any remedy needed at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we're now going to proceed, continue with your evidence. What I would like to do is in summary form outline the highlights of your political career and ask you to affirm whether what I say is correct. Mr. Kljuic, you joined the Croatian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina in March of 1990, and you served as the political secretary and acting president of that organisation until September of 1990. Between the 7th of September, 1990, and the 2nd of February, 1992, you served as the president of the HDZ BiH. Following the multi-party elections in 1990, you became a member of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and served in that capacity until 6 November 1992. You were again appointed to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and assumed that role from the 10th of October, 1993, until October of 1996. On the 6th of June, 1994, you founded the Republican Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a party which advocated multi-ethnic Bosnia, secular Bosnia, a democratic Bosnia, advocated the return of refugees. Between April of 1992 and October of 1993, you were the president of the state commission for gathering information on war crimes, and you remained a member of that body until the end of 1993. Currently, you are an advisor for foreign affairs to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that an accurate summary of positions that you have held and currently hold?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus, first of all, Mr. Kljuic, on your knowledge of and acquaintanceship with the individuals who were in the Bosnian Serb leadership, and specifically I'd like you to tell the Court, and I'll identify the person first and then I would like you to identify for the Court how well you knew that person, what the -- what contacts you had with that person. If we could start, first of all, with Radovan Karadzic. Can you describe to the Court if you knew Mr. Karadzic, how you knew him, how long you knew him, what your contacts with him were.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I knew Dr. Radovan Karadzic for about 25 to 30 years. He wrote a lot about cultural events. He was a doctor as well. For a long time we were members of the same football team in Sarajevo, on which he also served as a psychologist. At the time when political parties, national political parties came into being, our contacts took place almost on a daily basis until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And while we turn our attention to Ms. Biljana Plavsic. Can you tell the Court your contacts with her, how well you knew her.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I knew her family very well because for over 30 years I was a very good friend of her brother. Her I met a long time before the war, in Dubrovnik where they spent their holidays. Before the elections in 1990, my contacts with Biljana Plavsic were frequent because her brother insisted that we should be close, allegedly because we needed to assume joint stands, joint between the SDS and HDZ. Apart from that, we sat next to each other at Presidency sessions and saw each other practically every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of Nikola Koljevic, could you address your knowledge of him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I had known him for many, many years too. He specialised in Shakespeare, and his brother Sveto was also a lecturer at the Sarajevo University. All of them were people with whom I took part in many cultural events. And of course the intensity of our contacts increased in the preparations for the first multi-party elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Koljevic was also a member of the Presidency of Socialist Republic of --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. I spent many a day with him because we were members together in certain Presidency bodies such as the foreign policy committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally, let me turn my attention to Momcilo Krajisnik. Can you address how well you knew Mr. Krajisnik, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Krajisnik in 1990, during the election campaign. Later, when he was president of the parliament, we had a series of contacts, all the more so because as a member of the Presidency, I attended every parliament session. And in addition to that, in all major negotiations between the party, the SDS was mostly represented by Karadzic and Krajisnik, whereas I, at the time, was a leading representative of the HDZ. Apart from that, I spoke to Mr. Krajisnik several times in the course of official talks between the HDZ and the SDS. I wish to point out, however, that this political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina, starting from early 1990 to early 1992, was very condensed, very fraught. I cannot enumerate exactly how meetings we had [as interpreted], but that we knew each other very well, at least as politicians, is unquestionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me turn to the leadership in Serbia and have you address your remarks in respect of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It is evident that Slobodan Milosevic was the vehicle implementing a project that had been developed by the intellectual circles in the Serbian Academy of Sciences, and he was the first and only real leader that everybody had to obey one way or another. Concerning my political contacts with Slobodan Milosevic, I gave a statement when I testified in his trial. The subject of our conversations concentrated on efforts to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, to his great regret, I was not a good partner for that kind of agreement. We did talk, but there was no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you had numerous contacts with Mr. Milosevic and were able to ascertain from those contacts his views and attitude toward Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You couldn't really say that they were numerous, but we did have official talks, and in their framework we also had informal conversations. As for the policy of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic relative to Bosnia and Herzegovina, he did not hide his plans. On the contrary. He tried to find in me a partner for that sort of thing, as did Karadzic. However, I was an integrationist by conviction, as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina were concerned, and this is precisely the reason for my disagreement with the official circles in Zagreb. I was the first man to publish the national programme of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the most important thing in that programme was for Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain a sovereign republic, that is, to have the same status of the other former republics of Yugoslavia, a stand that was to be confirmed by the Badinter Commission. [In English] [previous translation continues]... finish. [Interpretation] And I sought equality for Croats in the then-Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'd like to remain focused, if I could, on the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. And can you identify the paramount leaders in the Bosnian Serb constellation of power.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Although officially speaking that circle was a bit broader, the greatest power and authority were wielded by Karadzic and Krajisnik, at the same time were the people relevant in our eyes. Biljana Plavsic and Koljevic occupied important state positions, but in the strategy of implementing the programme developed earlier, they did not have much say. Also, there were a number of other people such as Maksimovic, Buha, Ostojic, and others who were treated as members of the inner circle of the SDS leadership, but they exerted maybe some influence in the regions, certainly not in important issues of policy and strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could have a little less journalism in Mr. Harmon's questions. "Can you identify the paramount leaders in the Bosnian Serb constellation of power." This becomes almost lurid as a way of questioning a witness. There is a far more neutral way of expressing questions so that we actually get the witness's answers, and we do hope that if the phrase "paramount leaders" and "constellation of power" ever appear later in this case in any document it will be specifically noted that they first appeared in Mr. Harmon's question rather than in the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a perfectly appropriate way to ask the question. I can ask it a different way: Who are the most important leaders in the Republika Srpska. It's the same way of asking the same question. So the form of asking the question, Your Honour, I think is appropriate and I would like to proceed with the testimony of Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not find the form such that this would be inappropriate to put it to the witness. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you had an opportunity -- did you have an opportunity to observe Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic working together?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, that was no secret. Not only were they leading politicians, they were best friends. I believe in the entire Serbian leadership in Bosnia, the only sincere friendship was between Karadzic and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going to ask you if you could kindly describe the personal relationship as you knew it between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I said they were the only real friends, and that was confirmed by the leading positions they occupied. I can speak about that from my own experience and practice. When we spoke to SDS representatives, including Koljevic and Plavsic, and we agreed on something, that agreement could not be considered final. But when I spoke to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and we reached an understanding, we knew that that meant something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the actual position held by Mr. Krajisnik before the commencement of the war, he was the president of the Assembly. I would like to ask you your views. Was he -- did he have the powers merely of a legislator or did his powers extend beyond that? And when I ask you about those powers, I'm talking about powers within the Bosnian Serb party, the SDS, and the governmental structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness answers that question, could we be very clear, as we often need to be in relation to witnesses, if the witness is being -- well, there is expert evidence which this witness is not here to give. There is public record evidence. There are constitutional and legal matters and so on. Those are absolutely not what this witness is here to testify about. Of course, in the other area, the witness is then going on to give evidence of what he actually knows, what he saw and heard himself, then I can't object to that in principle. But I do wish before the witness even gets into these areas, with respect, to draw that clear, important distinction which runs throughout a lot of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you're inviting to keep it as much to the facts as possible, and of course the type of knowledge this witness has might make him not always entirely clear what would be expert testimony and what would be just testimony of a witness of fact that is related to his special position. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Kljuic, you have described earlier to the Court your extensive contacts and almost daily contacts with Bosnian Serb leaders and other important figures in the SDS party. You worked closely with Mr. Krajisnik. You had an opportunity to observe him relate to Mr. Karadzic. You had him -- you had an opportunity to observe his conduct in respect of other Bosnian Serb political figures on not only the national level but on the municipal level. My question is this: Based on your -- those facts, based on your knowledge of Mr. Krajisnik, having spoken to other Bosnian Serb leaders including members of the Presidency itself, are you able to inform this Court as to whether Mr. Krajisnik's authority within the SDS party exceeded those normal authorities vested in a Speaker of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that that was a period when for the first time in 50 years there was political pluralism in Bosnia. Political parties were coming into existence. We had no particular experience in politics. And most frequently, there would be interference between the official position one occupied and positions in political parties. I can tell you that Mr. Krajisnik was very skilful, that he was good at manipulating the agenda, that he could obstruct things that had been voted for. But every citizen of Bosnia can tell you that Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik were the top and everybody else was just the packaging.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So did his authorities, did his powers exceed those of a mere legislator?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, in political negotiations at the top of the party, he was at a significantly higher level than the one that he had within the state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are you aware of how his power within the Bosnian Serb political circles was viewed by Bosnian Serbs who were leaders of the SDS in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that question, how his power within the Bosnian Serb political circles was viewed by Bosnian Serbs who were leaders of the SDS in the municipalities, is not an appropriate question. If this witness has some knowledge which he can impart by evidence to the Tribunal of such matters of what Mr. Krajisnik's powers were in relation to the municipalities, what his links were with the municipalities, then he is legitimately able to give that evidence and then it can be evaluated. But for the question to be put simply in terms of how the people in the municipalities viewed Mr. Krajisnik's power, which is already a fairly vague concept, is really not the appropriate way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, that was not the question. The question was whether he was aware of how this was viewed. I take it that the answer will be yes or no, and if he was aware, then I take it that Mr. Harmon will come with further questions. And of course if the witness is asked about how others viewed a certain situation, then the course the Chamber expects Mr. Harmon also to explore on what basis he think he -- the witness thinks he -- knew what other people -- and how other people were viewed in certain positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the distinction Your Honour draws with a non-distinction, with respect, because the introduction "Are you aware," that is implicit in any question. Without the introductory words of the question "are you aware," the question is exactly the same. So the point is the same so my point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon knows what the Chamber expects him to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I simply want to make the point that the distinction that Your Honour draws is not a distinction which deals with my objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I said a few more things as well, and that was certainly related the basis of the knowledge of this witness. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question I asked you, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I know what the attitude was of the municipal officials, of lower-ranking officials with regard to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, he was very respected, because Mr. Krajisnik wielded a lot of authority. Apart from the high-level official positions that he had in Ergoinvest, the largest Yugoslav company, he was also respected as a good host. He liked to work on his property, and the image people had of him was a positive one. He was taken to be a good example in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is the basis of this view that other people respected him. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there was an incident in the field, I, as president of many Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, if I wanted to solve the incident in a given area, an incident involving Croats and Serbs, I would speak to Karadzic. He'd wave his hand and say that everything would be all right, but he never made a record of anything. But if I spoke to Mr. Krajisnik and said, "Let's solve this problem." If he agreed to do so, then rest assured that the problem would be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that still couldn't answer my question how you knew that the lower people could have been -- for other reasons that the matter was resolved. But how did you know how well he was respected by those on the lower levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was a journalist for many years, and there is such a thing as public opinion, and there's an attitude toward public opinion. Karadzic was the sort of spokesperson for those policies. He liked to speak to journalists. He liked to brag. He liked to issue threats. Whereas Mr. Krajisnik was a completely different type of character. He was very serious. He was very measured. He never gave statements that would irritate anyone. But he also implemented the general programme, and this could be seen in the Assembly. This is where it could be best seen. If we adopted an agenda that was of great importance for the state, you should know at the time the work of the Assembly was very intense because the society was in a transitory process. It was necessary to have reforms, new laws, et cetera. It was being transformed from a socialist system to a capitalist system. If the SDS didn't find this was appropriate, the president of the Assembly would give all 72 representatives the right to speak. The Assembly would then no longer have any purpose. The session would go on for a number of days, and we would end up without a quorum. So with regard to what the SDS advocated and with regard to the citizens who were in favour of the SDS at the time, with regard to these people, in their eyes, Mr. Krajisnik had a lot of authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still not a full answer to my question, but please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me explore also the authority -- your assessment of Mr. Krajisnik's authority during the war and after the war. Can you give us your assessment of his authority in those two periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, are we going to get facts? Because the way the question is put invites a repetition of the continuation of exactly the sort of answers we keep getting. It is terribly important that witnesses in the position of Mr. Kljuic are not steered by the questions towards some general statement of view which is very different from what they can actually tell the Trial Chamber they know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to explore that, but I kept getting interrupted. I asked Mr. Kljuic what his assessment was, and then I was going to ask him the basis of the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he should do it the other way round, Your Honour, because Mr. Harmon will continue to be interrupted, with respect, by me until he continues asking the questions in the correct form. And if he intended to do he should have avoided the question and gone to the correct, specific question first .

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe that is the correct form, Your Honour, and I would ask to continue with the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, whenever an assessment or an opinion on a certain situation is the subject of the question, would you include in your answer to the extent possible always on what factual basis your opinion or your assessment is based. So you now may answer the question, but please keep in mind this instruction. The question was your assessment of Mr. Krajisnik's authority during the war and after the war. So don't just tell us that he had a high authority but also on the basis of what you came to that assessment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina is aware of the authority he had. As far as the wartime period is concerned, I could not say because we were on opposing sides. But as for the post-war period is concerned, Mr. Krajisnik was the first Serb who was a member of the Presidency. He was also at the Dayton negotiations after Karadzic withdrew. One could say he had the support of the Serbian political elite. He was the most prominent representative. If you're asking me about the power he wielded, with the Prosecutor's leave, I with like to refer to a meeting that we had. I was an independent politician. I was pro-Bosnian, and the Serbian side kept accusing me of collaborating with the Muslims. And this was related to Zagreb. One day President Tudjman asked me why I wasn't cooperate with the Serbs. Probably because of the time that he had already established contact with Milosevic. I think that they had a telephone line in constant use. I arranged for a meeting of the Serbian and Croatian leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the Serbian side, there was the late Koljevic. There was Krajisnik and Karadzic. The meeting was held in Krajisnik's office in the Assembly. On our side, in addition to myself, there was the Minister Jerko Doko, and Ivko Stanic, my vice-president. That was a key moment at which it was possible to see the balance of forces. We, who were in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, wanted to recognise the borders of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, because if we did so then Bosnia wouldn't be an issue because no one would have any territorial desires. On the other hand, the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic recognised Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. As president I recognised Serbia Montenegro and Croatia. We had an important meeting between the leadership of the Serbs and the Croats, and I suggested to them, since they all said that I was a friend of theirs because I was very close to everyone, they said that it was very important to have me as someone born in Sarajevo, because in the HDZ leadership I had rural representatives, and they said it would be easy to reach an agreement with me. When I asked them, when I said that the only good thing for them to do would be to recognise the borders of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, they all stood up, all three of them, and said that this was not acceptable for them. That gave me the best argument, that gave me the best sort of proof that they didn't want to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina ago a state. They didn't want a peaceful solution. I could talk about the details of those policies later, but neither Plavsic nor Buha more Maksimovic weren't in front of me. It was the top leadership of the SDS, the first rank, and that showed how powerful these people were. There were certain images of certain people because that after a communist period that had lasted for 45 years. So this was the first time that people could see new faces at the political top. The newspapers would write about people's hobbies, about how they would spend their free time. So the media gave the impression, portrayed these individuals in a certain manner. And Mr. Krajisnik was portrayed as someone who had authority, perhaps because he didn't often appear in public. He was very cautious. He was very withdrawn, which wasn't the case for Mr. Karadzic, who was too extravagant. He always wanted to be the centre of attention. He made a lot of promises, he made a lot of threats, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, the meeting took place when approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meeting took place in autumn 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me focus -- I'm trying to focus your attention on the period of time during the war and after the war. And if I could have the next exhibit, which would be an intercept, and if it could be played. It is an exhibit that is found in the binder, 292. It will be found at the tab KID number 31423. Perhaps the usher could assist Mr. Kljuic in getting --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I haven't got anything on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If that could be turned to the appropriate page. It was again, I will repeat, KID number 31423. And if the Bosnian transcript could be placed in front of into Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did your honour find that particular intercept? Okay. I'm told it's -- do Your Honours' binders have KID number tabs on the side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and they --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are numbering from low to high, and my last number is 31272, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There should be a 31423. It is about halfway through the binder, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Halfway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a bit old fashioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see the numbering is not consistently -- yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to say it's a little get old fashioned, but what would be helpful for identification of intercepts is just to be given the date as well. These numbers are all very valuable, but the simple date is extremely helpful since that's how some of us work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect Mr. Harmon to give us the best possible clue for finding -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is an intercept, as it says on the top, dated the 27th of May, 1992. It has been identified in the spreadsheet. It's a conversation between Ratko Mladic and Mr. Krajisnik. And if we could have that intercept played. Could I just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We apparently have a technical difficulty, Your Honour. It disappeared from Sanction. So I think I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please try to get it back at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it's important to get it back. I see we're ten minutes before the normal break time. If we could have a break now and I can see if I can solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can have an early break now and begin again at quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to give some guidance from the Trial Chamber to the parties. The Prosecution is invited to explore, and I add to that, to the extent reasonable, the factual basis for any assessment of a situation the witness is asked to give. And the Defence is invited to at least give an opportunity to lay that foundation. The Chamber does not expect - I'm now talking about this witness - is that conclusions come into his mind today for the first time in his life. For that reason, the sequence, facts first, then the assessment, or assessment and then the facts, seems not to be of utmost importance. More importantly is that the factual foundation for the opinion or the assessment of the witness is finally presented. Mr. Harmon, technical problems having been resolved as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Miraculously, things were resolved in the time allotted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kljuic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will again, Your Honour, be paying attention to KID intercept, KID 31423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you should have a copy of a transcript of an intercept that you have listened to in front of you. It's the intercept that is dated the 27th of May, a conversation between Ratko Mladic and Momcilo Krajisnik. So if we could now hear that intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]. Mladic Ratko: Hello? Unidentified female: Hello. Mladic Ratko: Good morning! This is Mladic the General here. Unidentified female: Good morning! Mladic Ratko: Is Momir there? Unidentified female: Yes. Hold on a minute, please. Mladic Ratko: Please put him on. I need to speak with him urgently. Unidentified female: All right, immediately. Hello? Mladic Ratko: Yes. Unidentified Female: Here. The speaker is on his way. Hold on, please. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes. Mladic Ratko: Good morning, speaker. Krajisnik Momcilo: Good morning. Mladic Ratko: How are you? Krajisnik Momcilo: Well, okay. Did you sleep well? Mladic Ratko: I slept well. Look, I need to tell you that we have done our part at the airport deal totally, so it should be publicised. Krajisnik Momcilo: All right. Mladic Ratko: There are some individual shots there. They opened fire but we don't fire back. Krajisnik Momcilo: I'm doing that immediately this morning. Mladic Ratko: Yes. Momir is on his way down there. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes. Mladic Ratko: With these ... Boskovic and the others and they will be doing their job down there. Yeah, hello? Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes, yes. I can hear you. Mladic Ratko: I'm going further on as planned and tomorrow I will stop by to get new instructions. Krajisnik Momcilo: Excellent. Mladic Ratko: So we'll arrange for what we should do next. Krajisnik Momcilo: All right. Mladic Ratko: I have given Tolimir some instructions at the fronts and elsewhere everything is all right. Here I still don't have exact information on the area toward Ivan Sedlo but I hope we'll manage how to -- Krajisnik Momcilo: We have consolidated that Trovrh a bit. So it too is excellent. Mladic Ratko: That's excellent. I told Manljlo to strengthen it a little. Krajisnik Momcilo: You know, we have a kind of situation here. Mladic Ratko: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: It doesn't matter, it's just that this doesn't befit the Serb people. It can say much. Mladic Ratko: Yes? Krajisnik Momcilo: We are having a grand robbery of cars down in Vogosca. Mladic Ratko: Let's not talk about that. Oh, yes, yes. You should prevent that from happening. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes, yes, but let me just tell you -- Mladic Ratko: Yes? Krajisnik Momcilo: We have to send our military police this arrest these people. Mladic Ratko: No, no. Military police is not to be used like that. Krajisnik Momcilo: It's not to be used like that. Mladic Ratko: Don't do that, no. You have civilian police and let the civilian police do their job. Krajisnik Momcilo: All right. Mladic Ratko: There's also this -- Krajisnik Momcilo: These people doing. Mladic Ratko: ... in Zunovnica, Momo. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes. Mladic Ratko: In Zunovnica they steal military equipment and sell it to the Muslims. Krajisnik Momcilo: No, if we do things like this we will fail. Mladic Ratko: That's right. Krajisnik Momcilo: No way. Nor can these misdeeds be done by honest people. Mladic Ratko: There. Civilian police should take care of this. I told that same thing to that guy in Vogosca. They told me people from the Ministry of Interior should take control of this. Krajisnik Momcilo: All right. It's a deal. Mladic Ratko: This ministry and judiciary should do their jobs. Krajisnik Momcilo: General, every -- all people that have generals like you are lucky. Mladic Ratko: Let me ask you -- Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes. Mladic Ratko: What do you think if I gave a brief interview up there and call on younger pensioners? Krajisnik Momcilo: That would be excellent for the homeland, for the defensive war. Mladic Ratko: Excellent. Krajisnik Momcilo: There's no problem. Mladic Ratko: It's a deal. Krajisnik Momcilo: There will be a man up there who will join you as planned. Up there, at Sokolac. Mladic Ratko: Excellent. But let him come to that centre. Krajisnik Momcilo: He knows, he knows where too. You will be at the same place and he will be at Sokolac, you know. Mladic Ratko: All right. Krajisnik Momcilo: It's a deal. Mladic Ratko: All right. Krajisnik Momcilo: Bye. Mladic Ratko: Bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, first of all, can you tell me on May the 27th what in your view the context of this intercept relates to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, it relates to the subordination of the political and the military leadership of the Bosnian Serbs. Secondly, it is obvious that General Mladic was acting on political instructions. The problems that they had, for example the theft of cars in Vogosca and the looting that was carried out, is very characteristic for the first phase of the aggression. And finally, it's a fact that there was a sort of overall plan consisting of a number of stages. And on the following morning, Mladic was to find out what his next task would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in respect of the power and authority of Mr. Krajisnik, how do you interpret this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Although Mr. Krajisnik was officially the president of the Assembly of Bosnian Serbs at the time, it's quite clear that he had a lot of influence in day-to-day tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell me in the intercept where it says, "I will stop by to get new instructions," what is your views as to what that illustrates as to Mr. Krajisnik's authority?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, the authority wasn't just official. It wasn't just based on the position that he held, because one would assume that the president of the Assembly would be involved in legal matters. But it's clear that events in the field developed in such a way that it was necessary for the very top or for the Serbian leadership to supervise all actions, to lead all actions including military ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the intercept it indicates and I quote: "Mr. Krajisnik, we have consolidated that Trovrh a bit. So it, too, is excellent." What is Trovrh?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, Ivan Sedlo is a significant point on the road from Mostar to Sarajevo. And from Ivan Sedlo, its it's possible to control the traffic on the road. And Trovrh is also one of the elevations in the vicinity of Sarajevo, and it obviously had a lot of military importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell me your views as to what Mr. Krajisnik's knowledge of the situation on the ground reflects.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously he was well-informed, if the chief commander of the Serb army was reporting to him and seeking instructions, or at least very often if not every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I've conclude with that intercept. Let me ask you now: We were focussing on his power, Mr. Krajisnik's power and authority, and you had contacts with him after the war ended. Can you very quickly and succinctly give us your views as to what power and authority Mr. Krajisnik had, and can you give us the factual basis on which you base your views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What time period is the question directed to? Because -- that might be helpful, because Mr. Harmon has referred to Mr. Kljuic having had contacts with Mr. Krajisnik after the war and then it's not clear what period as far as Mr. Krajisnik's power and authority are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was talking about after the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that is now clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, could you kindly answer the question. After the war, what authority and power did Mr. Krajisnik have, and can you tell us on what you base your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I did not have contacts with Mr. Krajisnik during the war, because I was never in the BH delegation during the war at negotiations in Geneva or Dayton. However, I know that Mr. Krajisnik was part of the leadership of the Serbian delegation. After the war, in 1996, I left the Presidency, and I was a parliamentarian for four years whereas Mr. Krajisnik was elected in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina but he never wanted to enter the building of the Presidency. Instead, the first meeting of the Presidency was held in a restaurant. Later on, every following session took place in the land museum. It is interesting that Mr. Krajisnik was the only one of four members of the Presidency who didn't want to enter the building of the Presidency, although everybody who was elected knew that there were supposed to work in that building. Since after Dayton Accords were signed, Karadzic could not occupy a political position. Having been eliminated by Americans from political life, and that was one of the conditions of the Dayton Accords, Mr. Krajisnik became officially the leader of Bosnian Serbs. His stance after the war and after the aggression were no different than the stance that he had advanced before the aggression, at least when the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, together with equality among peoples, the return of refugees, indemnification of victims, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'd like to turn to an entirely different topic, and that is your observations and conclusions about the SDS party itself. Based on your contacts with the political leaders, based on your contacts with members of the SDS party, can you tell the Court how the party itself functioned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, it was more a military organisation than a political one. It was not democratic. It did not recognise the principles of political dialogue. Instead, it set an objective that was unacceptable to others. Namely, in political life the freedom of one political organisation is restricted by the freedoms of other similar political organisations. When we came into power, it was primarily needed to change the political regime from socialism to some sort of democracy. All controversial issues needed to be agreed upon in the parliament. However, that did not happen because of the ultimatum imposed by the Bosnian Serbs not only on other peoples, other nations, but on all the citizens who did not support their policy. Later, we would get a major confirmation that not all Serbs were in favour of Karadzic. And when a referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared on the 22nd of March, 1991, a great number of Serbs -- possibly a third, and there would have been even more if the referendum had not been declared on the entire territory did support the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the most important institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina worked directly against that state's interests. Namely, we wanted to reach a political understanding with the other former republics, and that was completely normal. The understanding was to be that Bosnia and Herzegovina should have the same status --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're going to get into that. I would like you to stay focussed on the question I asked you, and that question is, essentially: Can you describe to the Court, based on your experiences, based on your observations, how the SDS party functioned, if you're able to give us that answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I said very clearly it required military discipline and within the party there was no dialogue, to wit, they had their own programme which was part of Milosevic's general programme. In order to break up Yugoslavia, Serbs in Croatia, in Eastern Slavonia, in Knin, were activated first. Bosnia and Herzegovina's turn would come later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you're going beyond the question that I asked you, and I'd like to try to stay focused on the question. Let me ask you, in terms of the SDS policies that had been created, what role did Mr. Krajisnik have in ensuring that those policies were implemented? Can you give us your views on that, and then can you tell us on what you base those views.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Very well. I said that the SDS policies were not pluralistic. They had a programme that was part of Milosevic's general programme, and those Serbs who would not accept those policies were proclaimed to be traitors. I have to say that the number of such Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were significant, as we would later see in the parliament. For instance, when we decided to seek independence, the Serbs from the SDS walked out, but Serbs from other parties such as communists and reformists stayed at the session, and a number of Serb deputies voted in favour of independence. The policy of the SDS was two-phased. They had, on the one hand, Milosevic's global programme, and for a while, before they had prepared for the aggression, they conducted talks and allegedly sought consultations and negotiations about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, trying to create an impression with the public opinion that they wanted to solve the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina. While within the framework of all institutions such as the government Assembly, et cetera, we discussed general issues, they secretly prepared arming themselves and preparing documents such as stage A, stage B, et cetera, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: -- that testified to their insincerity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not clear how that answer is getting anywhere near the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's why I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we probably were both just choosing the same moment to run out of patience on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, I would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'd like you to very carefully listen to the question I asked and then if you could focus on the question I ask and give the Court the answer to the question, it would be helpful because we will get through the examination very efficiently. I have a limited amount of time in which to present your evidence, and I'd like to do so as efficiently as I can. My question to you is: What role -- if you can give us an answer on this. What role did Mr. Krajisnik have in ensuring that SDS policies were implemented?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: His role was crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You see, he was at the head of the Assembly for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he held 72 per cent of SDS deputies under control. On all issues, including some very trivial issues that did not involve political or national interests, those deputies always voted the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what role did Mr. Krajisnik have in that process? If you know.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In the process of destruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Starting with the implementation of SDS policies?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have already said that he played the main part, in view of the fact that Karadzic kept higher profile and took a greater part in negotiations with all sorts of negotiators that passed through Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. In the structure of the SDS itself, Mr. Krajisnik had no match, and that was a fact well known to every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence -- in one of your answers you mentioned that the -- the word "traitors." And let me just draw your attention, if I can, to the use of that term within the context of what we're talking about, and that is SDS policies. And I draw your attention and the Court's attention to comments of Mr. Karadzic from the 8th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. These are found in -- this is Exhibit 65, binder 8, tab 93, and let me quote Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Kljuic, to you, and let me get your observations about this quotation. And that is Mr. Karadzic: "However, once the party has adopted a policy, anything else is treason. Anything outside the adopted policy is treason. Assisting the enemy cannot be tolerated, giving him a way out and confusing the people while being a member of that party of the Assembly and the party organs. This cannot be. I will not allow it. I will signal to the people, people, this man is a traitors. That is what I will do in the future." First of all, Mr. Kljuic, do you have any observations or comments about what Mr. Karadzic said on the 2nd of February, 1992, or at the 8th session of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course. Since a significant number of the Serbs, the majority of the citizens, did not agree with Karadzic's aggressive policy, nor could they accept a forced division of ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it is impossible except through violence and crime, Karadzic, in order to ensure the untouchability of his own party and its status, required that this programme be universally accepted. One member of the Serbs never accepted it and remained with us in Sarajevo with us during the aggression. Because that programme consciously accepts military objectives without any alternative at the time negotiations were under way primarily concerning the future of Yugoslavia. The leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina in its entirety accepted that Bosnia-Herzegovina could stay if Croatia and Slovenia were staying as well. If those two republics were not willing to stay and that turned out to be the case later --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, again, I was only asking you about your comments and observations as to the quotation that I read from the 8th session of the Bosnian Serb assembly. I think we're going beyond that. Let me, therefore, continue with the examination. You mentioned that some Serbs did indeed stay with the government after the Bosnian Serbs left the parliament. What was the attitude of the Bosnian Serb leaders, including Mr. Krajisnik, if you know, to people who were Serbs who did not adhere to the SDS policies?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: They were treated as traitors. And to tell people that somebody is a traitor means condemning that person to isolation and to certain consequences that "irresponsible" citizens could inflict on that person and his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik share the view that the persons who did not subscribe to the SDS party views was a traitor?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could play the next intercept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Harmon, I would like you to lay a factual foundation for the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you have an opportunity to observe Mr. Krajisnik in his relations with people who were not -- who were Serbs but were not SDS members? Can you describe his views and attitude toward those people.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He, just as Karadzic, condemned those people as traitors of Serbdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, could you give us, just like we saw a quote of a speech given by Mr. Karadzic, would you have similar factual observations and then specifically relating to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Presidency and in the parliament and in the government alike, certain Serbian representatives remained, and they always complained that Karadzic and Krajisnik were threatening them for allegedly committing treason against Serb interests. It is not an insignificant number of people who were concerned, and those people held important positions. For instance, after the walkout of the SDS in the beginning of the aggression, there were three Serbs in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Miodrag Simovic, as deputy prime minister, who stayed on for a while longer before leaving; and the Minister of Justice, Ranko Nikolic, who stayed throughout the war in Sarajevo. And he stayed even later on after the war. And there was Mr. Kovac, Minister of culture, who also stayed throughout the war. And he became later ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Paris. There are some Serbs who also stayed in the parliament. There are specifically two Serbs who replaced Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic and later Mr. Kecmanovic. These people remained in the Presidency, and they were with me every day, namely Mirko Pejanovic and Tatjana Lujic, both university professors. And there was a Serb, Miro Lazovic, acting as speaker. All of them constantly complained about threats issued against them from Pale, these threats saying that they should leave their positions because they do not represent the Serbs. Some of these people took part in negotiations in Geneva, and Lazovic was involved in Dayton Accords negotiations as well, were told by Milosevic, whenever he came, that, "I don't want to see these people. They're not Serbs. They're Izetbegovic's Serbs." So that sentence "that anybody against this programme was a traitor" pursued two objectives: One, for the programme to be implemented unquestioningly; and second, to label anyone who did not support the programme as a traitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have heard in the question a quote by Mr. Karadzic. In your answer, you've told us that threats came from Pale. Then you gave another example how Milosevic treated them. The question, however, was about Mr. Krajisnik. So did they tell you that they were threatened by Pale? Did they tell you that they were threatened by the SDS leadership or by Milosevic or by Karadzic? Where did they -- did they ever, and then please explain to us, did they ever specifically mention in this respect Mr. Krajisnik? Because that's what this question is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. I cannot say they specifically named him, but the word "Pale" was a synonym for the Serbian leadership of Bosnian Serbs. And I know for a fact that there were some people who kept in touch with both Pale and specifically Mr. Krajisnik on the one hand, and Sarajevo on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. If we could go to the next exhibit. It's an intercepted conversation dated June the 26th. Your Honours, it is found in the binder at KID 31472. That's about two-thirds of the way through the binder. When Your Honours have found it, I will proceed with the actual playing of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we then have the intercept played, please. Your Honour, there appears yet again to be a technical problem. We will come back to this intercept in a few minutes when the technical problem is solved, and I'll continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kljuic, we're going to return to an intercept that's before you. You can -- I would like to direct your attention to another portion, another subject. The Court has heard a lot of evidence, and there's no reason for you to recount that evidence, about the contacts and the cooperation that existed before the multi-party elections. Likewise, the Court has heard considerable evidence about the manner in which the structures of government were formed after the multi-party elections, when Mr. Krajisnik became the president of the Assembly. What I would like to focus your attention on, and focus it specifically at this point in time, is on the respective platforms of the SDS, HDZ, and the SDA in respect of the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina in a disintegrating Yugoslavia. Okay. So first of all, Mr. Kljuic, can you tell us what those positions were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, after 45 years of a single-party system, for the first time political parties came into existence, some of which were of a nationalist kind. But there were also other parties, reformist parties, liberal ones, and parties of post-communist orientation. All the platforms were acceptable. A problem arose with regard to the implementation of these platforms. The SDS platform, at the beginning of the 1990s, was a very democratic one. However, this is one of the consequences of the communist regime. People in the former Yugoslavia are used to saying one thing but acting differently. A problem arose with regard to discussions of the future of our common state. Most of the western part of the former Yugoslavia wanted a reformed Yugoslavia. They wanted it to be transformed into a sort of confederation in which central power would be constituted of five elements, the army, the police, the customs office, the diplomatic office and financial department. This is something that Milosevic did not like, and discussions commenced. And because of Milosevic's attempt to take over power in Yugoslavia, there were increasing conflicts. The Slovenes and the Croats, although they initially didn't have a plan for independence, after the unsuccessful talks demanded independence. Bosnia-Herzegovina could not remain in a rump Yugoslavia, because that would have been tantamount to a Greater Serbia.
