So the SDS then issued an ultimatum: Either remain in Yugoslavia, or we'll split up Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since according to the constitution Bosnia-Herzegovina was equal to all the other republics, we discussed the matter. We said we can't remain within Yugoslavia, but we can form a democratic Bosnia and Herzegovina in which no single ethnic group will be threatened. At the time, I was president of the HDZ, the Croats' political party, and they were in the minority in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But instead of finding a compromise in the Assembly, and instead of finding a manner of Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond protecting national interests, and in order to do this we suggested a Belgian model in which each three people would be represented by a -- some -- a body called the Council of People, and they would have the right to veto any law or decision that would pose a threat to the people concerned. However, the SDS did not accept this proposal and on the one occasion Karadzic stated that either the will of the Serbian people would be accepted or they would deal with the matter in a military manner. The will of the Serbian people is not an element contained in the constitution, and I'm not going to address the matter as to whether the entire Serbian people had such a will. And this is what led to the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But the entire situation was unfolding on two levels. There was the public and political level, and the other level was the one represented by Milosevic and the JNA and a group of nationalists from Serbia, because before Bosnia-Herzegovina had been internationally recognised on the 4th of April, the JNA units inundated its territory. They had been withdrawn from Slovenia. And then there were the reservists who came from the JNA from Serbia and Montenegro. There were paramilitary Chetnik formations led by Arkans and Seseljs. And finally there was the well-armed Serbian people who had been armed by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you again to come back to the question. Can you distil for the Court what the SDS position was in respect of Bosnia -- the status -- future status of Bosnia and Herzegovina? The Court's heard a lot of evidence about the history in this case of the -- and they've heard about a number of elements you've described, but I'm interested in your describing to the Court what the SDS position was in respect of the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was very clear. Bosnia-Herzegovina had to remain in Yugoslavia at all costs, or it would no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the position of the HDZ and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Naturally, we were in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question is: Which citizen of any country in the world would not want the independence of his own state after a period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The whole necessity for this sort of evidence is that if there is one fact among others in the case which has been very clear for a very long, long time, it's that the SDS wished Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. With everything we have to deal with in this case, it does seem that this witness is being invited to cover a great deal of ground which is now simply not in issue at all and is perfectly well known. We wouldn't have any objection if it's really thought for some reason important to have this as a feature of this witness's evidence, then I would positively invite Mr. Harmon to lead quickly through some of this absolutely well-known material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the Chamber has heard a lot of evidence indicating that the position of the SDS was that they wanted to remain within Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, that the SDA and HDZ preferred to have an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. If there's anything new you would expect this witness would tell us, please ask him, but otherwise, I think not only this position but also some explanation of these positions, that is fear to become a minority and an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina which could be -- are explained as well extensively, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am aware, Your Honour, that this has been covered considerably. This was a foundational question to get to other matters. I was interrupted by Mr. Stewart to get to other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have led the witness in this respect: "Would it be fair to say the position of the SDS was," and you repeat what is in evidence, because it took us two pages of transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Based on your conversations, Mr. Kljuic, with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and other Bosnian Serb leaders, did they describe to you what would happen if there was not a resolution to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina? What was it they said to you would happen?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, everyone knows this, and they didn't conceal it. Karadzic even publicly stated this in the Assembly. He said that if the will of Serbian people wasn't accepted, and he wasn't referring to international constitutional law, he said that if in such a case one people would disappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm again going to stop you. The question was what they told you in the conversations you had with these gentlemen. If Mr. Harmon would be interested to say what kind of public statements were made, he'll certainly ask you. But please listen carefully to the question. Your conversations with Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and other Bosnian Serb leaders. Did they describe to you what would happen? So the focus on the question is on your conversations with them and what they told you, and not what was commonly known. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In conversations that I had, they would say the same thing. They said if this isn't done, our will will be done. It wasn't a secret. It was something that was made quite public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did -- you are fully aware, Mr. Kljuic, of the positions that were taken by Mr. Krajisnik about Bosnia. You're very aware of what the consequences were if those -- that position was not adopted. What did Mr. Krajisnik tell you would happen to Bosnia and Herzegovina if the Serb position was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: His opinion didn't differ from that of Karadzic's, but that evening when we were in the Assembly in Mr. Krajisnik's office, he said that this was something that the Serbian people would never accept. That meant that they would never accept an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Only an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina could have been a solution for all the three peoples, naturally providing that the constitution guaranteed their equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still, Mr. Harmon, this does not answer the question. The question is not whether Mr. Krajisnik accepted it but what he said would happen if the Serb position was not accepted. So did he say, "Well, we'll live then happily together for the rest of our lives," or did he say, "We'll go to the joint European Union," or did he say, "I'll pray for a better future"? That is the question: What if not accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them only said one thing. They said the Serbs have a solution if you don't accept our positions, and this position was an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the ultimatum that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Either there will be Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia or part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Western Herzegovina will be part of Croatia, and all of us will join Yugoslavia. And these were problems that recurred on a daily basis in relation to these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was war ever considered to be an option to solving the problem in the Yugoslav context?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on the basis of leading to that particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question may be put to the witness. The objection is denied. So the question was whether war was ever, you said, Mr. Harmon, ever considered or was mentioned as a consequence of non-accepting the Serb position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] War was also part of the ultimatum. According to their plan, it was necessary to separate the Serbian people from the other two peoples. Anyone who has any knowledge about Bosnia and Herzegovina knows that this is impossible. This idea wasn't even accepted by all the Serbs. However, by making all the preparations for an aggression, even when negotiations were very intense, they would stir up incidents to see to what extent we were prepared for resistance. In February and in March 1992, there were a number of large-scale incidents in Sarajevo at key points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again. The question is whether in your conversation, as I said, whether war was ever mentioned as one of the options. And then you explained to us that this was more or less implicit in their plans. The question was clear. Did they say, "We'll go for war," or did they say this: "This and this is what had happen, that this part will join this entity, that part will join --" and it was your opinion that this could not be achieved without war? So, did they mention the war or was it your conclusion that war was inevitable in order to achieve those plans?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these plans can only be implemented by having recourse to the military. They can't be implemented through political means. They didn't conceal this. They had two rehearsals before the aggression, and this was done at the locations where the upper part of town was supposed to be cut off from the lower part of town. And in the upper part of town, that's where all the state institutions were located. If they had cut this off, the lower part of town couldn't have existed. So they did not conceal the war option in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand your testimony properly, that is, it was your conclusion that it could not be done without war, and you found this confirmed in, well, a -- in an exercise you observed take place. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony? I see you are nodding yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read to you a quotation from the Bosnia-Herzegovina 10th Assembly Session that took place on the 11th of March 1992, and let me just get the exhibit number. It is Exhibit 65, binder 9, tab 107. So this is March, before the war, and let me read to you Mr. Karadzic in quotation. And he's reporting back to the Bosnian Serb Assembly about the conference in Brussels, and he says as follows: "Fortunately, Europe realised that a conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina was what was needed and that nothing done against the will of one ethnic community could succeed in Bosnia and Herzegovina; i.e., that such action could lead only to uncontrolled processes and chaos, the result of which would be a bloody civil war with hundreds of thousands dead and hundreds of destroyed cities, after which would -- we have the same situation as we have now with three Bosnias and Herzegovinas. But only after a war and with much less population in cities which would be completely, ethnically homogenous, for it must be assumed that the forcible and bloody removal of minority peoples from one region to another would be carried out on a large scale in a civil war." Now, this is Mr. Karadzic speaking on the 11th of March. Can you comment on this quotation that I have read and put it into context with what had been said to you by Mr. Karadzic and by Mr. Krajisnik prior to the commencement of the war.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This is a very clear position expressed by the SDS leadership. However, it's not based on the constitutional law. However, it's not based on the constitutional law. On the other hand, they would never have spoken in such a way if they hadn't prepared a military force. You must be aware of the context within which this took place. After the JNA withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia, it came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, which at the time was an area with the highest concentration of military force in Europe. It was necessary to negotiate under such conditions. On the other hand, the question of the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina wasn't an issue. It had existed for centuries, even when it wasn't an independent state in the Austrian Empire and in Turkey. It was a separate administrative entity. The terms used by Karadzic, "if there is no Yugoslavia there won't be a Bosnia-Herzegovina either," is not a true statement because Bosnia-Herzegovina is an old state. Through the last hundred years it has a standard established border, whereas Yugoslavia existed as a democratic monarchy and one year after it was unified it became a absolute monarchy. It was a state that existed on the basis of an agreement. So this statement illustrates the message that Karadzic gave to us before the war. But in order to understand the message and its force, you must be familiar with the action that they took prior to that event, prior to that message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. But in your negotiations where you were trying to resolve the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the SDS party, the Bosnian Serb leadership, you mentioned, for example, Mr. Karadzic giving a speech in October in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Let's listen to that speech. We will listen to that speech, and then I will ask you some additional questions about it. This is -- I'll just organise this here from this end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, it would be time to take a break. We apparently have another difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technician suggests, Mr. Harmon, to come and assist, because they think there should not be a real problem. They, of course, can follow on the screen what actually is done at this windows ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we still need a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still need a break. I'm just figuring out if we have the usual break now of 20 minutes whether we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually I can make one suggestion. While we try to resolve the issue of the film, I'm told that the intercept that was unavailable earlier can be played now if that would give us additional time. It breaks up the examination and the manner in which we're proceeding, but we have so many technical difficulties and problems today that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Well, let's have the 20-minute break now. That means we will adjourn until 20 minutes past twelve, and then we'll continue without further interruptions until a quarter to two, and could you please make sure that there is an alternative programme for next phase of the technical facilities. We adjourn until 20 minutes past twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Harmon, the final technical solution has been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We hope so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, before the recess, we were focusing attention on the Bosnian Serb position in respect of the status of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was asking you questions about the position of Bosnia -- about the position of the Bosnian Serb party if their position was not accepted, and I read to you a quotation from Dr. Radovan Karadzic on the 11th of March, 1992. I would now like to play for you a video of a speech given by Dr. Karadzic in October in the Assembly. If we could played that. If it could be audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, usually for the transcript it is -- the text is translated. It wasn't now because we only could read the English text on our screens. On the other hand, I think that this video has been played before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, at this moment the -- we'll find the translation of the part just played in the transcript of the previous playing of this same part. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, was Mr. Krajisnik present when that speech was given?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. He chaired the session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you present when that speech was given?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the reaction to that speech?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Whose?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the -- your reaction? What was the reaction of the non-Serb parties in the legislature?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a slightly ambiguous question. Perhaps Mr. Harmon could -- does he mean the immediate reaction, there and then on the occasion, or does he mean the wider reaction or does he mean both? We'd suggest it is too general at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of the reaction was audible, visible but audible. But, Mr. Stewart, I think that this position we could first how the witness understood it and then see what additional questions to be put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, what was the reaction to that speech in the non-Serb communities, both in the parliament and outside of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This statement not only revealed Karadzic's true intentions, it also caused consternation not only among Serbs but among all the citizens who couldn't possibly expect such an announcement of evil, because this reaction, in view of what had been done by Slovenia and Croatia, was completely normal. The European Union asked us whether we wanted independence. And I ask again: Is there any citizen who wouldn't wish his country to be independent? Yugoslavia had been compromised by the hegemony of Serbs, but most prominently by Milosevic. That was visible in all the institutions of the system, especially diplomacy, the media, the police, and the army. The people who had any sense of equality and any sensibility for equality did not wish to remain in a Yugoslavia of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what did -- what were you informed -- having negotiated with the Bosnian Serb leadership and having had daily contact with them, what were you informed specifically of what areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina were sought by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Serbs had claims that went beyond any imaginable principles. They invoked all sorts of historical periods and eras, claiming that certain territories belonged to them, even when those territories had never, ever been populated by a majority of Serbs. That concept, that design, was known under the name of Greater Serbia, which involved a territory in Croatia from Zadar and Karlovac, which was 50 kilometres away from Zagreb, and Virovitica, which is in Slovenia. In all the negotiations with Croats in Zagreb and with Croat representatives in Sarajevo, they gave freedom to Western Herzegovina, which had a clear majority Croat population, because in the structure of the new Croat state, the Herzegovina lobby was very influential. So their territorial claim was absolutely unnatural and impossible. However, in view of the power they had in the army, the police, the media, and in view of the preparations they had put in place, they considered it normal to put such ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the territorial claims, let me show you next exhibit. It is a map. If we could have the map shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit number P293.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, before you have a copy of a map based on the ethnic distribution in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, you said the territorial claims made in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina were impossible. First of all, how did those territorial claims in the negotiations affect the distribution of people within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There are two important points here. The map shows territories, but this is not a realistic picture because a great number of these territories are almost unpopulated, or are half-populated. Serbs had the majority in 31 municipalities out of the total of 110 in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In certain municipalities they had a relative majority. But all of this was significantly below their claims. In other words, they claimed even the territories where they were not even the second largest group. This would become evidence in -- evident in Brcko, which was populated by 44 per cent Muslims, 25 per cent Croats, and 20 per cent Serbs. However, in all their proposals, they wanted Brcko for themselves. In some other areas as well, such as Foca and Prijedor, where Muslims were in the clear, overwhelming majority, the Serbs made similar claims. And some of these territories did end up in Republika Srpska. All this goes to show that the ethnicities were so intertwined in Bosnia and Herzegovina that division was impossible, even if you grant a one-year period for families to move to other places. All this could only be effected with huge sacrifices involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if the Bosnian Serb position in respect of the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not accepted, we have seen what has been forecast by Mr. Karadzic in the 10th Assembly Session. I read a quotation to you from that. Mr. Karadzic has expressed himself in October in the Bosnian Serb Assembly session. I'd like you, Mr. Kljuic, to tell this Court what Mr. Krajisnik said to you and what Mr. Karadzic said to you if the Bosnian Serb Assembly session -- Bosnian Serb position was not accepted. You've described ultimatums. I'd like you to touch upon those ultimatums that were made to you, and I would like you to be very specific and focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, that's inappropriately leading. Mr. Harmon asked the witness to tell the Court what Mr. Krajisnik said to him and what Mr. Karadzic said to him. That would have been better divided up, actually, as it happens, but the point is that then to say to the witness, "You've described ultimatums," and then introduce the word "ultimatum" into the question in that way, even if he has referred to ultimatums at some time in his evidence, that is really significantly leading, to introduce a word like "ultimatum" in that question and quite unnecessary in the sense that if the witness is able to give evidence on this, he doesn't need and shouldn't be given a such word in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm asking him about the ultimatums he received very specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question -- the question focusses on what the witness earlier said about ultimatums and otherwise there's a serious risk that the witness will tell us whatever was said by Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik. So since the witness used that word before, it's not improper to focus the question on that issue. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you can answer the question. If you'd like, I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It is no secret that they made ultimatums to us. Similarly, it is no secret that the Serb leadership never said, "If you don't accept the will of the Serb people as formulated by SDS leaders, there will be war, there will be devastation," and so on. It was their answer in any discussion about a peaceful solution to the Bosnian crisis, a crisis that should never have existed in the first place. Namely, we used to live in a relatively well-organised state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are commenting on the situation, but you're required to answer the question. The question was: When you say that they expressed themselves in terms of ultimatums, what was then said to you, not whether it was -- whether crisis should have existed or not. The question is simply what did they say to you at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just what I said before. If we don't abide by the will of the Serbian people, there will be war. And I must tell you the hardest night we had was after Karadzic's speech at the Assembly. A very heavy atmosphere descended upon us. And in the hall of the Assembly we tried to talk and to explain certain things. The situation was so fraught, so sensitive, that the Assembly continued discussing only at 5.00 a.m. the next morning, after we had spent that entire night in the Assembly trying to find a compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the beginning of your answer says just what I said before. "If we don't abide by the will of the Serbian people, there will be war." You earlier explained that these were not the words used in your conversations but that you concluded from what they said that war would be inevitable. Now, the question, was if you're talking about ultimatums, what did they exactly tell you? Because it seems to be a bit inconsistent with your earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, these contacts were frequent. They were daily contacts. And I just told you that after Karadzic's speech, we spent the following seven hours in the Assembly talking, trying to save the situation. Always, at all times, and they never hid that, they had one and only ultimatum. It's either going to be as they say or Bosnia and Herzegovina will not be. It was not a diplomatic discussion, it was an open talk just like in a green market.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you were talking about the topics with Mr. Karadzic, for example, or Mr. Krajisnik, for example, topics of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you understand that when Mr. Karadzic was talking to you he was asserting the position of the SDS party? Likewise, when Mr. Krajisnik was talking to you on that same subject, did you understand him to be talking and asserting the SDS position to you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course. They propounded the stance of the SDS with the proviso that Mr. Karadzic was more aggressive, more egocentric, more open, whereas Mr. Krajisnik was more tactful, calmer in discussing certain details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the speech that was given by Mr. Karadzic on the 11th of March -- I've quoted from it earlier, I'll requote a portion of it. The last sentence that I quoted: "For it must be assumed that the forcible and bloody removal of minority peoples from one region to another would be carried out on a large scale in a civil war." Did Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, touch upon in their conversations what would happen to the non-Serb people who were living in Bosnia in territories that the Serbs wanted?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It is clear that they envisaged their own fate, that they would come to a bad end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. In the discussions that you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, did they discuss with you what would happen to the non-Serb peoples who were living in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territories that the Serbs coveted? Did they tell you what would happen to those people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course. They forecast the fate of those people, namely that they would have to leave those territories in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And what you -- and when you say "in one way or another," can you explain that to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the question -- Mr. Harmon quite correctly, if we may say so, started off by focussing in this series of questions on what was actually said, but at this point we shift in Mr. Harmon's question and ask the witness to explain, and that's an unfortunate shift because if we were to stick with what the witness can say was said, the questioning would proceed in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather clarify this issue. You said that they forecast the fate of those people, namely that they would have to leave those territories, and then your last words were "in one way or another." Is that -- are these the words they used? Did they say "in one way or another?" Or is this just a summary of what they said? I'd like to know that first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was their message. And it was very strongly confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was whether these were the words used. Did they say "in one way or another," or did they explain? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They only said they would leave. I said "in one way or another." And an argument in corroboration of that was the way the Serbs cleansed those areas where they had seized power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what -- what may have happened afterwards, but not, I take it, at that moment what was told to you in your conversation. So they said they would have to leave. How did you understand this, what you said was a message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no dilemma whatsoever as to their wishes. We had experience from Croatia, and they end of the day one part of the people, Croats and Muslims who lived in villages and towns with a majority Serb population already in the second half of 1992 started fleeing from those areas. The threats were made on a daily basis, at work, at school, in shops, because tensions were heightened intentionally in order to create incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's of course a different matter from what was said in your conversations, I mean, what happened in the shops and the schools, et cetera. So I'd like to know from you where you said a message was went to you and that the words that they had to leave not in one way or another, on the basis of what did you understand this to be a message that whatever would happen, there would be -- they would have to be out of those territories? I just want to know what made you draw that conclusion. Was it the wording? Was it the other experiences? What is -- because you linked this to what was said elsewhere. Well, whatever, but I'd like you to explain to us why you understood this to be a message that whatever would happen, whatever means, whatever, they would have to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By heightening the tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, an aggressive structure of people appeared in the ground -- on the ground, especially in areas where Serbs were the strongest, and they started preparing others for an exodus. For instance, in infirmaries, in hospitals, in schools, people -- non-Serbs in senior positions were replaced by Serbs. That was when power was being seized unofficially. And people did not need additional explanations as to what would happen when power was seized officially. Everybody in Bosnia and Herzegovina knew that. You didn't need to say it in so many words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me put into context, if I can, your remarks when you had these conversations with Mr. Krajisnik, with Mr. Karadzic, that the non-Serbs would have to leave one way or another. What had happened in Croatia in respect of non-Serb populations prior to the war breaking out in Bosnia? And did those events have any relevance on your understanding of what Mr. Krajisnik and what Mr. Karadzic were telling you about the non-Serbs having to leave one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was our principle argument and, unfortunately, our tragic experience. And most importantly, they publicly supported what was going on in Knin, Dubrovnik and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "they publicly supported," who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The leadership of the SDS, the entire leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what had happened in Croatia in respect of the non-Serb populations who had been living in territories that were claimed by the Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think you have very good evidence in the Tribunal. And as everybody knows, there were crimes, rapes, killings, deportations, expulsions, always accompanied by actions pursuing material gain such as seizure of property.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Had there been ethnic cleansing in Croatia, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Not only did it exist, it was the only aim of that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In conversations with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, including Mr. Karadzic, did they point out -- did they discuss what happened in Croatia with you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did they say to you in respect of what would happen -- what had happened in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I held a speech in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina at a session chaired by Mr. Krajisnik. In that speech, I said that all of us had to distance ourselves from the crimes and the ethnic cleansing taking place in Croatia. Some MPs from the SDS were laughing. I said they shouldn't be gloating. They shouldn't feel triumphant about this evil, because I personally was horrified that this suffering was taking place in Serbian towns, and I referred to Cacak, Valjevo, and others. I also said I couldn't understand them. How could they have no empathy at all for the victims? And this lack of empathy for the victims would continue to be typical of them, to this very day. You know, in Bosnia, people suffered a great deal. This suffering will never be known to the public at large, because in many instances all the witnesses were killed. But I have to say, Your Honours, there were people in Bosnia-Herzegovina who cried out loud, "Don't do this. This will be a crime forever." However, this feeling of power manifest in the media, in the police, and in the army imbued them with a false sense of superiority, and they could not be stopped in those intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked what they said to you. You're now describing a lot of things that have got nothing to do with the question any more. In the beginning I was waiting, because you said what speech you made, how they responded. That's still not a direct answer. But then you just start -- and I'm not saying it's not true and it's not relevant, but it's not the question. And then you start telling us about the suffering of the people, and of course this Tribunal pays a lot of attention to those aspects of the case, but it's not the question put to you. So I again instruct you to listen carefully to the question and not give a kind of general commentary on the situation but just to answer the question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me be very narrow and precise in my question, Mr. Kljuic. We have been discussing the issue of ultimatums. You have told us that in your discussions that you had on a daily basis with the Bosnian Serb representatives, in the discussions you had with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, they said that the non-Serb people would have to leave in one way or another if their solution was not accepted. I asked you about the context, what had happened in Croatia before, and you stated there had been ethnic cleansing in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to summarise so I can get to the point, Mr. Stewart. So if I can finish before --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, an accurate summary is essential in the exercise and I thought that the whole point of exploring this matter was to see what these men did say --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I was getting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Harmon has already said in his summary they said that the non-Serb people would have to leave in one way or another. That is precisely what this whole line of questioning -- in a frustrating way for everybody, I quite agree -- is designed to establish. So to incorporate that in a summary is to lead the very conclusion that everybody is wondering that we will reach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Things can change. You insisted in one way or another on being part in what was said before been now it's a different situation. Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's totally different, Your Honour, and it's unfair for Your Honour to suggest I introduced that phrase because it's a wholly different point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Witness, you told us that in the conversations, the frequent conversations, you were told that the non-Serbian population had to leave those territories claimed by the Serbs. Was what had happened in Croatia one of the reasons why you understood this to be an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were no secrets, if Karadzic said in six months prior to the aggression, if he said this in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that after the events in Croatia, and on the basis of the behaviour of the leadership of the Serbs in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you could not at that moment understand those observations on the basis of what happened later, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But given the daily conduct of the Serbian leadership, I thought that this is what would happen in Bosnia too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say what happened in Croatia, and as you just explained on the words used by Mr. Karadzic during his speech where he said they would have to leave, you gave it -- at least in your opinion this had a specific meaning. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier in one of your answers you referred to people fleeing Croatia. You mentioned the second half of 1992. Is that what you intended to say? What did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatia, this all took place in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the reason why I'm asking you. So you say what happened in Croatia, and you referred yourself to Croatia. You wanted to refer to the latter half of 1991 and not as it appears in the transcript in the latter half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It therefore is in this context that you understood the words all non-Serbs had to leave in your conversations with not yet very much specified but with the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition, I was a member of the state Presidency, and I was the president of the party, and I would receive information at the state and party level from the field. I received information on the status of Croats in areas where the Serbs were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, in your conversations with Mr. Krajisnik, when he was discussing with you the consequences that would ensue if the Bosnian Serb position about the future of Bosnia was not accepted, did you explain to him that such consequences would be unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Naturally. Not just myself. Many people said the manner in which the SDS acted was an impossible matter in which to act in normal and peaceful circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he aware, Mr. Krajisnik aware, of the consequences that war would bring if the Bosnian Serb people tried to assert their position forcefully in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What do you say -- on what do you base that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I should first of all tell you what the relationship between Karadzic and Krajisnik was. Karadzic was more aggressive, more bombastic, and he articulated their objectives at greater length, whereas Krajisnik didn't speak much. However, on one occasion, Karadzic told all of us -- he was addressing the core circles, the core members of the SDA and the HDZ and the SDS, he said, "Be aware of the fact that the Serbs will do what they intend to do, and the international community will, in the end, support the side that is the strongest one."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that statement made in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik, either on that occasion or any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said in the course of the debate that was occurring on the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina that both the Serbs had one position, the Croats and the Bosniaks had a different position. The Bosniak position was in favour of sovereignty. At the same time those discussion were is going on with the SDS party in which you participated, in what Mr. Krajisnik participated, what steps were being taken by the Bosnian Serbs to ensure that their position would prevail?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: On the one hand there were the political negotiations, either within institutions, the Presidency, the parliament, the government, or there were bilateral or trilateral party leaderships. And on the other hand, on the other side, there were preparations for an aggression, which were supervised from Belgrade with the assistance of the JNA, the police, the media, financial institutions. And later, paramilitary formations joined them too. The purpose of the negotiations was to portray them as people who were interested in finding a peaceful solution to the problem, whereas the technical preparations made for the aggression had as their -- the motto was that they should be as arrogant as possible in those negotiations, that this is a picture reflected from the top echelons of Yugoslavia. And after reactions such as the one in Croatia, the chances that Yugoslavia would survive diminished. So given our starting point, our desire for a reformed or a transformed Yugoslavia -- that was our starting point, but because of their threats, we ended up with a desire for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. If this hadn't been the political will just of the leaderships of certain citizens' parties, the HDZ, et cetera, this will be demonstrated by the referendum at a subsequent date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. At the same time that there were negotiations on the fate of Bosnia that were taking place between the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS, were the Serbs being armed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was arming the Serbs during that period -- during the period of time prior to the destruction and the break-up of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Primarily it was the army, but there were other sources too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You're referring to the JNA. Can you give us a concrete example that you know of the JNA actually arming Serbs? The Court's heard a lot of evidence about this subject, but I'm asking you for any examples that you can tell the Court, very specifically.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I knew the gentleman whose name was Vlado Stopjic. Vlado is an interesting name because both those of the Orthodox faith and of the Catholic faith use this name. He was a very capable man. He was a businessman, and he had a fruit juice factory and a big house in Lukavica, which is a suburb of Sarajevo and which is inhabited mostly by Serbs. One morning in front of his house, he saw a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher, three or four cases of weapons, and it was packed in green cases and had "JNA" inscribed on it, which shows that it was from the JNA. It also had various codes inscribed on it. This took place a few months before the aggression. And he found a Serb in Croatia, and they exchanged their properties, and he moved to Croatia. He was one of the more intelligent men. But the fact that there were weapons provided by the army is not in dispute. There's an interview given by General Kukanjac. It appeared on the Serbian television in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he expressed his dissatisfaction for having been forgotten after he had retired. He said, "None of this would have happened if I hadn't armed them."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. General Kukanjac, just identify him, his position, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the army region which covered most of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he had his headquarters in Sarajevo. And he was the commander of the 91st in 1991, up until the beginning of 1992, when he was replaced by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to a document that you're familiar with, the variant A and variant B document. And I won't take the time to show it to you. I know you have seen it before. But let me ask you -- I would like to quote from Mr. Karadzic. This is a quotation from Mr. Karadzic at the 50th Bosnian Serb Assembly Session held on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995, in which he refers to variant A and variant B. I'm going to read it to you, and then I'm going to ask you for your comments? "At the moment the war began, in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, municipal boards, municipal assemblies, presidents of executive boards. You will remember the A and B variants. In the B variant where we were in the minority, 20 per cent, 15 per cent, we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander." This is a quotation, for the record, from Exhibit 65, binder 12, tab 128. Mr. Kljuic, can you comment on the variant A and the variant B documents and what that suggested to you was happening at the same time negotiations were occurring to resolve the problems in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we suggest a bit more foundation needs to be laid here to establish, for example, when Mr. Harmon asserted the witness has seen variant A and variant B. No doubt he has in the course of some preparation, but when he saw it. Some link between this witness and that document needs to be laid as a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it should be clear whether the witness at that time had any knowledge it and how he understood it at that time or how he interprets it with the experience he gained since that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, are you aware -- have you seen the variant A and variant B document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how did you interpret that particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's not good enough, Your Honour. We don't know whether he saw the variant A been B document yesterday because he was shown it by the Prosecution or in 1990 something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He answered he saw it before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. My apologise for overlooking that. But nevertheless, with that recognition, nevertheless something more specific is required. Because we've had evidence about variants A and B when certain people say it was produced. It is important to be specific about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Witness, at this moment you may proceed on your line of questioning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we could show the witness variant A and variant B, and I could have -- and it's found in Exhibit 65. It's in 65, binder 6, tab 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Kljuic, you've seen this document. How did -- how do you interpret this document any time when there were negotiations ongoing to resolve the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the game being played by the SDS at two levels. First of all, they were negotiating, asking for equality, et cetera, but in secret they were preparing for an aggression and they were arming Serbian civilians. It's not a secret. The document with version A and version B was familiar even before the war. I think it comes from the end of 1991, but towards the end of January or February 1992, we had this document at the Presidency. You must know there were parallel institutions, and many intelligence officers and policemen remained loyal to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was a document, the application of which was very broad. It's not something that could be concealed. So we were aware of their plan for variant A and variant B. And to how well it was prepared, you can see this very well in the case of Brcko because that was plan B, and they took over a certain percentage of the town and expelled a certain amount of Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, these instructions are dated the 19th of December, 1991. What is this -- what else occurred on the 19th of December, 1991, that was significant?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That evening we had a meeting of the Presidency, and it was a very important one, and it was necessary to extend the term of office for the president since according it our constitution one representative of the seven equal members of the Presidencies would be selected, but it was only possible to preside for one year plus one year. On the 19th of December, 1991, Mr. Izetbegovic's mandate expired. He could extend it for a year. He had the opportunity to do so, although that morning Karadzic tried to distract me, but I didn't accept that. He attempted a form of sabotage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, please don't interrupt me, then. It was very important to replace Izetbegovic in order to stabilise Bosnia-Herzegovina. Karadzic suggested I should be the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said, "Well, how?" He said, "It's no problem. There will be two Serbs and two Croats. That amounts to four votes. And perhaps Fikret Abdic will vote for us too." Formally, it was possible to do that. And if I were someone else, I could have agreed to being president. But at the time, I had already split with Zagreb because of the policies conducted with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And secondly, if I were elected as president, it would have been necessary to rotate the president of the government and the president of the parliament, because if you know -- as you are aware, there were three representatives from three peoples, the three key positions, and such a change would have caused a certain crisis in power, because who knows whether they would have agreed to have someone else appointed in the place of Krajisnik as president of the Assembly. Who knows whether they have agreed to have Jure Pelivan, the prime minister, replaced. And perhaps the idea was to bring me in, as I had no influence over the population apart from the fact that they respected me as a citizen. But I didn't have any real influence over the masses and I wouldn't have been able to command the army and police. Also Bosnia-Herzegovina didn't really have any weapons. Later there was a form of arming, assistance from the side, et cetera, but these things I couldn't get involved in. And finally that evening we were supposed to make a request for a referendum to be held on independence. And while we were working on this at the level of the state leadership, in the morning they distributed the document containing variant A and B. They distributed it in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like you to direct your attention also to any other events that were happening, Mr. Kljuic, that were -- that you interpreted as preparations for war by the Serbs at the same time they were discussions with and between the various political parties to resolve the crisis in Bosnia. Did the Bosnian Serbs create parallel governmental structures? Did they create their own Assembly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What about the events -- what about the common means that were available to support the Bosnian people, the SDK, for example? Were there any actions taken in respect of them at the same time there were discussions to resolve the matter of Bosnia? And can you explain what those actions were.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps you're not aware of the fact that in the socialist system, all financial transactions were conducted via a service called the SDK. They thus maintained financial control over all transactions. And one of the instructions contained in variant A and B was to take those funds and to keep funds in areas where the Serbs were in the majority. And what is most important is that all the reserve food in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all the reserve weapons - and this was not an accident - all these reserves were in areas where only Serbs lived. So in making these preparations, they took everything they could take from what was jointly owned, not only because this was in their own interest but because they wanted to prevent others from acting. And while this was being done, this greed and this looting, was something that their power structure did. Later, all those people who left had to hand over all their property to the Serbian parastate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to another topic and that is the issue that we touched upon a little bit earlier, and that is whether or not Bosnia could be divided ethnically, whether you could separate the Serbs from the Croats and the Muslims. And you've told us that that was not possible. Did you have such a discussion with Mr. Krajisnik? Did you tell Mr. Krajisnik that fact?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were a number of discussions. There was a tete-a-tete that we had in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in his office, and we suggested a peaceful solution. If this peaceful solution was refused, there was only one alternative, and that was war. And I must say that the tragedy of the Bosnian Serbs is that they had partners for peace, because no one wanted to go to war apart from themselves in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina can't be regarded as consisting of only Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. There were a lot of people who didn't have a national identity, who didn't characterise themselves in nationalist terms. There were some people who didn't think that the nation was an important factor. But the most difficult thing was that there were very mixed marriages, mixed in terms of religion and ethnic affiliation. And the children issued from such marriages could not opt for just one identity. This was clearly evident when you have a look at their names. Children from mixed marriages would take neutral names which didn't reveal the ethnic community to which they belonged. On the other hand, the fact that the population was mixed -- the population was mixed to such an extent that in one skyscraper you'd have 80 Muslim families, 50 Serbian families, 20 Catholic families, two Jews. And no one would agree, and no one would -- no one would agree to leaving Sarajevo and going to a village where his ethnic community lived. Apart from that, the citizens' parties that had 18 per cent in the election -- 18 per cent of the votes in the elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was: Did you tell Mr. Krajisnik that Bosnia could not be divided along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I did. Not only Mr. Krajisnik. I said that to many people lots of times. It was unimaginable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Krajisnik's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I've already described the rhetoric of Krajisnik and the rhetoric of Karadzic. Krajisnik did not have much need to speak when Karadzic was voicing everything that both of them thought. Karadzic made a lot of threats. Krajisnik never did. However, when Karadzic made that speech in the Assembly, Krajisnik, as the chairman, did not stop him. He didn't say, "What the speaker is saying is inappropriate."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, again, is: When you told Mr. Krajisnik that Bosnia could not be divided along ethnic lines, what was his reaction to what you told him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He was silent while Karadzic was saying, "We will do what we will do, and the international community will recognise the force of the stronger party."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How often did you tell Krajisnik and Karadzic? Did you warn them that Bosnia couldn't be divided along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Please, this is no longer an issue of recognition or acknowledgement. If somebody says something like that a hundred times, you can't forget it. On the other hand, I have to tell me we had joint meetings of all the institutions, for instance, Presidency, parliament, and government, where we wished to discuss outstanding issues. However, those outstanding issues could not be resolved in any parliamentary way because of their ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was just how often, be it ten times, be it 50 times, be it a hundred times. That was the question. Do I understand you correctly that it was at a high frequency, because you mentioned at least somewhere in your answer that if something said a hundred times. Was that -- is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if this will mean anything to you, but I said that a number of times. I didn't count. But it was imperative in our life at the time to repeat it: Please, don't go ahead with force, please. All of us will end up suffering. Let's not going to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I mention at this point, Your Honour there are two or three matters for which I would need about five minutes, but if that helps the Tribunal with a view to timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going to play an intercept that lasted 6 minutes and 49 seconds, because I thought I had ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it you would like to put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was going to be the intercept I couldn't play this morning. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm hesitant, because if it can be played now, at least it shows that we have no technical problems in respect of this. So therefore, with the approval of the interpreters and the technicians, also keeping in mind that we started the last session rather early, that means if we're running out of tapes it's over anyhow... Please do that, Mr. Harmon. Also, let's try to get the answers as concrete as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put this intercept in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We were interrupted, Mr. Kljuic, because of technical problems. We were discussing the view of Bosnian Serb leaders in respect of Serbs who did not adhere to or follow or subscribe to the SDS policy. And if I could play this following intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the interpreters are requested to say it into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, for your sake, it is found in tab 31472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's the date, please, Your Honour? Or through Your Honour, what's the date, please, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: June the 26, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Mandic Momcilo: Hello. Miljana: Minister, how are you? Just a minute, the president would like to talk to you. Krajisnik Momcilo: Hello? Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Hello? Krajisnik Momcilo: Mandic. All right. Are you a traitor as everybody else? Mandic Momcilo: God forbid. Hello? Miljana: Minister, the connection broke up. Mandic Momcilo: Something at your end. Miljana: You can talk now. Mandic Momcilo: From the village up there, and then you get cut off. Krajisnik Momcilo: Hello? Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: Momo? Mandic Momcilo: Yes, President. Krajisnik Momcilo: What was it? Mandic Momcilo: Probably something at your end. Krajisnik Momcilo: The moment I told you and you betrayed that you are a traitor. The line got cut off. Mandic Momcilo: God forbid. I would never do that. Krajisnik Momcilo: Momo, tell me, how is it going? Mandic Momcilo: Well, I'm not up-to-date with what's going on in the lower part. The main one but as for this one it's going well. Krajisnik Momcilo: These haven't come in at all. Mandic Momcilo: Not at all. Krajisnik Momcilo: No. Mandic Momcilo: I wouldn't know anything about that. Krajisnik Momcilo: It's a shame, a shame. Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: Two things. Actually, I wanted to see if Stanisic was there, to see with him what was going on so it means that we all agreed -- that what we agreed upon was not respected. Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: There's still half a chance today and tomorrow I will finish. Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: It's a big problem with Alija, has that one been finished? That is awful. As of today we finish it all, you know. Mandic Momcilo: Here there is something pounding. Krajisnik Momcilo: Uh-huh. Mandic Momcilo: It could be heard that they are pounding. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes, that's it. Has he made it down there or not? It's all over now. Secondly, have you released the one I told you about by any chance? Mandic Momcilo: Yes I have. Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes? Mandic Momcilo: He left for Vrbanja one hour ago. Krajisnik Momcilo: Thank God. Mandic Momcilo: Karamehmedovic, that's right? Krajisnik Momcilo: Yes, that's him. Mandic Momcilo: Well, he's gone. Krajisnik Momcilo: Let me also ask you about that Savic Milos. It's his brother that's really... Mandic Momcilo: President, I put it on the list. The first next exchange and it will be finished. Krajisnik Momcilo: Check it down there. Do you have anyone there? Can you contact someone? Mandic Momcilo: There is this Vukovic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb who is criticising us because we are -- we have 400 prisoners here, you know. Krajisnik Momcilo: Who is criticising? Mandic Momcilo: I've got 400. Krajisnik Momcilo: And who is criticising? Mandic Momcilo: This Filip Vukovic, member of the youth organisation. Serb, he says. Clean it, but for them they are -- Krajisnik Momcilo: Filip Vukovic, you say. Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: Communist. Mandic Momcilo: Yes, yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: What does he want? Mandic Momcilo: He is president of that Exchange Commission. Krajisnik Momcilo: Their commission? Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: And what is it that he wants? Mandic Momcilo: War prisoners. No, they are ex- for them. They are hardly interested in people. They are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children to go to Vrbanja, to go to their own people. He says that's ethnic cleansing what we're doing. Krajisnik Momcilo: Does he now. Mandic Momcilo: Here when -- Krajisnik Momcilo: And where is he now? Mandic Momcilo: There somewhere. I don't know. Krajisnik Momcilo: With them, isn't he? Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: That means he's one of them. Mandic Momcilo: Yes, yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: God, traitors are all around. Mandic Momcilo: Yes, yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: Good, Momo. Look, please do call him. I would like to help Savic. It's his brother at stake. Mandic Momcilo: First exchange I will take care of that. Krajisnik Momcilo: Good, Momo. Mandic Momcilo: And that man, is he gone? Krajisnik Momcilo: Momo, let me ask you something. Mandic Momcilo: Yes. Krajisnik Momcilo: Who should we appoint the republican prosecutor? Slobodan Avlijas? Mandic Momcilo: Yes. It is -- President, here there is a man who knows everybody who is from here. Krajisnik Momcilo: I know him. Mandic Momcilo: So you know him too. Good. Krajisnik Momcilo: If he was pro-judge -- Mandic Momcilo: He was -- he was in my ministry. However, he is skilled, capable. He knows many of those people and the place doesn't hold him. I think he is the right man for it. Slobodan Kovac, that one will not do. Krajisnik Momcilo: Slobodan Kovac, that one will not do. Mandic Momcilo: Slobodan Kovac? What? Krajisnik Momcilo: Good. Mandic Momcilo: Already. Krajisnik Momcilo: You should draw up that proposal and sent it from there. Mandic Momcilo: Deal. Krajisnik Momcilo: All right. Mandic Momcilo: Bye. Krajisnik Momcilo: Come on, go back to work. You are hardly there yourself. Listen, you say I will fax you and you do it straightaway. You say I will give you the phone number, and you do it straight away. We should set you free from this fax because -- Mandic Momcilo: Don't. Will come. Krajisnik Momcilo: You don't have to. Mandic Momcilo: Skrbo is here. I don't know what to do with him. Krajisnik Momcilo: Don't go to the field now. Mandic Momcilo: No, no, no. President, what are we going to do? Send a commissioner to Kasindol, two, three men, some Papazi. They came to me from doctor Avramovic from Kasindol. Nobody ever called. They scattered away over there. They appoint their own people, directors. Krajisnik Momcilo: And who is that one? Mandic Momcilo: Kasindol, the hospital. Krajisnik Momcilo: Who are those people? Where is that coming from? Mandic Momcilo: Local community of Kasindol, the Crisis Staff. Krajisnik Momcilo: And is that a municipality? Which one? Mandic Momcilo: It's the local community of Ilidza. Ilidza is the municipality. Kasindol is local community. Krajisnik Momcilo: And why do they have the Commissioner? Why don't they go there? Mandic Momcilo: No, it isn't. I don't know which. Those doctors came to me. They appointed some Sonja Divljan instead of this corrector. Krajisnik Momcilo: And how could they do that? Mandic Momcilo: This Crisis Staff of the local community, Kasindol, appointed her. Krajisnik Momcilo: Come on. Mandic Momcilo: And then Koviljka Popovic, the cashier, to make an overview to see how the income is being distributed in income again. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will now call Prstojevic to go there and to send somebody because he has the Crisis Staff in Ilidza and that is Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter hasn't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we have not received the full interpretation of the intercept. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I said please proceed, it's for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic identifies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we first have for the transcript to receive the full English interpretation of the transcript. So I think that we finished approximately with Popovic Koviljka. Is that correct? I'm asking the interpreters to finish the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Mandic Momcilo: It's a shame, President. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will see that they take care of that immediately. Mandic Momcilo: But they are in contact with Prstojevic. Krajisnik Momcilo: See, then, if he doesn't do anything we will have to send someone else there. Mandic Momcilo: They are in some kind of business with that Prstojevic, black-marketeering or something. Krajisnik Momcilo: He cannot do anything on his own. He has the committee now some wonderful people are there now, you know? They aren't the old ones any more. Mandic Momcilo: But Doctor, these came and they are whining and crying. Krajisnik Momcilo: Tell them it will be taken care of properly. Mandic Momcilo: Because they're not obeying. They didn't give them a slice of bread. Krajisnik Momcilo: Who? Mandic Momcilo: Those from the local community because -- Krajisnik Momcilo: Who is not giving them a slice of bread? Mandic Momcilo: They would not allow assistance to go straight to the hospital in Kasindol but only through them. Then they stopped that assistance, aid, and then they gave them a little. It's a disgrace. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will now -- Mandic Momcilo: People should be arrested, President. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will find Dragan Kalinic now to go there and see what needs to be done. Mandic Momcilo: Yes, please, Doctor, do call. Here I have five people sitting here right across from me staring at me and -- Krajisnik Momcilo: Momo, what you were promised I will do. Mandic Momcilo: Good, President. Krajisnik Momcilo: There is no such Minister in the entire planet. Mandic Momcilo: Oh, come on, please. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will -- Mandic Momcilo: So they don't disperse the staff. Krajisnik Momcilo: I will, Momo. Mandic Momcilo: Thank you very much. Bye. End.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I played this intercept for you in the context of your previous testimony that dealt with the attitudes of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik and other attitudes toward non-Serbs who did not subscribe to the SDS agenda. Can I have your comments on observations in respect of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: We see in this conversation the drastic qualifications they give to people who are not towing the line. Although there is an error in the identification of Filip Vukovic. It's true he is a communist, but he's not a Serb. He happened to be a Croat. We see from this that they were sending women and children to us, which is another result of ethnic cleansing. But if you wish, we can also see from this that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in many problems beginning with exchanges with the Muslims, because this person, Karamehmedovic, had been sent to Sarajevo, and in exchange some people were demanded from Sarajevo. Another detail: The hospital in Kasindol -- that's a small place, Kasindol, and there was some local problem there. It was not natural to involve the Speaker of the Assembly in such a small local problem. Anyway, that's the way it happened. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kljuic, this concludes for today this hearing. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. That will just be checked whether it's in the same courtroom or not. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're still about to give. And may I ask you specifically for tomorrow to carefully listen to what is the core of the question, because I'm fully aware that you could tell us far beyond what you're asked to tell us. But we have to stick mainly to the questions. So therefore, may I ask your specific attention for that. You're excused. Madam Usher, please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first point is this: I ask that Mr. Krajisnik could be supplied with -- and I don't one know whether it's a tape or a disk, a tape or CD -- but if Mr. Krajisnik this afternoon could be supplied with the audio of today's proceedings in B/C/S so that he is able to review Mr. Kljuic's examination today and what he said about intercepts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand, Mr. Stewart, it takes -- if we have been here for five hours, it takes five hours to play it and get it on another medium. I don't know what could be done so that at least he might have it this evening, but it would certainly not be before 7.00, because we are in Court for five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, 7.00 would be better than not at all, Your Honour. It's not ideal, but of course it will be about an hour before Mr. Krajisnik gets back there anyway and if he were to set aside some of his evening for that, well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will try to do our utmost best. If you could please get in touch -- keep in touch with the registrar to see what is possible and what is not, but I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The second point is this: On the list we were supplied by the Prosecution this morning there's a CD relating to authenticated transcripts. We haven't been given that, but I wondered if we could be given that or the opportunity to burn a copy of it, that would be most helpful. It obviously exists because it's listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this CD mentioned on the list, is it there for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which list is counsel referring to? If I could have a copy of that, I could respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the list which we were provided with this morning, the list as of October 26 [sic] setting out the various exhibits the Prosecution intended to call. It's the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Stewart, which list because we provided with you a lot of lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 2 on this list is "CD containing authenticated transcripts."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I referred specifically to this list we were supplied with this morning. My apologies if that didn't identify it specifically enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the list in relation to Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed that we are -- will prepare that and we will provide that to the Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This afternoon. Could we have a -- I don't want to be too demanding but some time target?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have that information at hand. I'll get it to you as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's say three times the times it means burning a new CD. Is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 4.00 would be satisfactory, Your Honour. It seems reasonable, gives plenty of latitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last point is this, Your Honour, Your Honour has made a decision last week about a question of closed session and obviously I'm going to be careful about what I say in open session about that. This is the last day on which we could apply for a certificate under Rule 73(B).
