We are going to face a practical problem over the next couple of hours as well, Your Honour, that the printers and computers are not going to be available to us -- this is bad day for technology. They're not going to be available to us for technical reasons. Your Honour, it would take me about one minute to make my application to Your Honours now, because really there is essentially one Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond point as the basis for that certificate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should then turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not necessarily, because I won't identify the witness. The point is a point of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's simply this, Your Honour: Your Honour in your judgement, which has been given openly anyway, the decision said that "the Defence seeped to be under the misapprehension that the Chamber itself is obliged too see original evidence of the objective factors before it may form an opinion." Your Honour, that was not our misapprehension and not our submission. Where we say that the Trial Chamber has gone wrong with respect is a matter of fundamental principle is the Trial Chamber required enough evidence to be satisfied that there was the basis for saying there was an objective risk or objective danger. Where we, the Defence -- of course Your Honours will disagree, but then after all, we're talking about an appeal, when, we submit, that the Appeals Chamber might agree with us that the central point is this: That what Your Honours didn't do, we submit, and we still -- did submit at the time, but we do say that the Trial Chamber was wrong on that -- didn't allow us to pursue the matter to see whether on further reasonable inquiry that prima facie position, that the Prosecution had met the threshold of establishing an objective risk, might in fact then be neutralised by further inquiry. And we do say, Your Honour, with respect, that it was unreasonable for us to be stopped from pursuing the matter with the witness to establish whether one looked at the totality of that "readily obtainable evidence," whether the overall balance would have been in favour of interfering with the prima facie right of the accused to have the matter dealt with in public. And we do urge that this is a matter on which -- important point on which guidance should be sought from the Appeals Chamber and that it is a matter of principle here. And although Your Honours' position is Your Honours' position and by definition you won't agree with my submission because you have ruled. But it is exactly the sort of point on which an Appeals Chamber might very well take a different view. It is an important point. And it is would, of course, in principle it does materially advance a trial if something which should have been dealt with in closed session is then, as a result of an appeal ruling, dealt with or opened up then for open session. So it is an important point, Your Honour, and in this case we do urge that a certificate would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. This is an oral application for certificate --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For a certificate under Rule 73(B), Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Rule 73(C) says the ask for certification will be filed within 7 days which at least suggests that it should be a written submission. But if it would help you, of course, I do understand that you have previously explained it already and perhaps on the basis of that explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes. And I think Your Honour has a general -- the Trial Chamber has a general power to dispense with that specific requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of your explanation, you're granted an additional day for filing the written application for such certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, is it true that you would like to address the Chamber? It seems that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to say a few words about this witness, more specifically regarding the material I received. There is a small number of witnesses whom I know and with regard to whom I could assist my own defence. I have received no material whatsoever except for one written statement. I didn't receive any intercepts or transcripts or anything. And my participation is very passive. I would like to be enabled to participate, because this witness got dates wrong and years wrong and mixed up meetings. I would like to be able to say that to my counsel so that he can put it to the witness. You will understand that I'm very unhappy because the Prosecutor says he gave this to my Defence yesterday. Yesterday was Sunday. And it is technically impossible for my counsel to consult me. He can only do it in the afternoon, after the testimony, whereas it would be logical for him to consult me before the testimony. Your Honours, you will appreciate this is a very complex case. You know this better than I. It would be a good thing to enable me to participate in my own defence. There are certain things I am technically unable to point out to my Defence counsel. I'm sorry that I am taking the floor here, but I do have to object to this situation of complete confusion, and the technical difficulties I have with consulting with my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say I didn't know Mr. Krajisnik was going to say anything today but in this case I utterly support what he said. I did have in mind to review overnight so that we could inform the Trial Chamber very specifically, particularly in light of the conversation this morning, what the timetable had been with the supply of material. Because it is, without going into -- it's a wholly unsatisfactory situation and way of dealing with these matters. But, Your Honour, I undertake to sort out overnight -- Mr. Krajisnik has in fact -- the only thing I disagree with he has in fact been supplied with some material by us on Friday, but so far as the intercepts are concerned, before the weekend all we knew was there were 137 or 138 intercepts from which some selection would be made. So we did not make our own guesswork selection of what it would be. But, Your Honour, we will get the facts straight overnight so that we can assist the Trial Chamber to sort out any residual difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as was said in the beginning of this hearing, that the Chamber would closely monitor how the examination of this witness would go, it was not the easiest one until now, and certainly we'll keep in mind there as well the concerns expressed by Mr. Krajisnik as far as preparation is concerned. And as I indicated before, we'll finally see how to find a remedy for difficulties incurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just -- I would like to make the record abundantly clear, Your Honour. The intercepts -- all of the intercepts, I am told -- were handed over to the Defence in June of this year. Then, Your Honour, I identified -- and I'll correct -- and I'll get that date in just a moment. Then I was informed, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 2.000, of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. There were a large body of intercepts that were turned over to the Defence on the 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 17th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have a dispute, but it's either a day difference. But let me just say, Your Honour, 137 intercepts were then provided to the Defence as the possible pool from which the exhibits would be identified. On the 24th of September, I identified 21 of those exhibits to the Defence, and because we had to translate the comments on the remaining ten intercepts that formed part of a spreadsheet, we had those translations completed and on those ten were sent over to the Defence, I believe, yesterday afternoon. So that is the history of the intercepts. I'm just trying to find out whether transcripts as well were turned over to the Defence in June. I will inform you accordingly. But I think it's important to put on the record the facts that relate to the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd just like to say that rarely does one party so cogently make the case against himself by that description of the timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the appreciation of the time is quite different between the parties. The Chamber is more inclined to concentrate on how to solve the matters, because the Chamber has an open eye for both the difficulties the Prosecution is facing but at the same time also the difficulties the Defence has to resolve, and in order not to add another difficulty, that is that we are running out of the tapes, we will adjourn until tomorrow morning. Madam Registrar will do her utmost best to get the tape or at least the audio material of today's hearing available to Mr. Krajisnik, and we'll finally see how the further preparation, to what conclusions that will lead and whether any specific solutions should be found for that situation. We will adjourn to -- until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
